questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $y=sec⁡x?$

- $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ is in the domain.
- $x=\pi $ is a root. $$
- $y=\frac{1}{2}$ is not in the range of the function.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's plot the graph of $y=sec⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934039/assets/da729794a0331383debd75be0a4ce4a9f2d4da3286f50bd4f284868996077412.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- Statement I is false. The function is defined for all real numbers except the values $\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $ for any integer $n,$ thus it is not defined for $x=\frac{3\pi }{2}.$

- Statement II is false. The function has no zeros.

- Statement III is true. The range of the function is $(-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ),$ so $y=\frac{1}{2}$ does not belong to the range.

questions.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Secant Function
questions.worked_solution:
The period of $y=sec⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=4$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2\cdot 4\cdot \pi )=sec⁡(x+8\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $sec⁡x=3\sqrt{3},$ then $sec⁡(x+8\pi )=3\sqrt{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Secant Function
questions.worked_solution:
The period of $y=sec⁡x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=5$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡x=sec⁡(x+2\cdot 5\cdot \pi )=sec⁡(x+10\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $sec⁡x=\frac{5}{2},$ then $sec⁡(x+10\pi )=\frac{5}{2}.$

Finally, then

$$
\begin{aligned}4sec⁡(x+10\pi )-3 & =4(\frac{5}{2})-3 \\  & =2(5)-3 \\  & =10-3 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Evenness Property of the Secant Function
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the graph of $y=sec⁡x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934039/assets/fbf6ef1ca91f998ab4dc2dda1890ffc8a713f2eeff19e5569351b2466256d63a.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of $sec⁡x$ is $2\pi .$

- Our graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis. This means that $sec⁡x$ is an *even* function, and we have

$$
sec⁡(-x)=sec⁡x.
$$

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of $sec⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡(-x+4\pi ) & =sec⁡(-x+2\pi \cdot 2) \\  & =sec⁡(-x).\end{aligned}
$$

- Secondly, using the evenness of $sec⁡x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡(-x) & =sec⁡x \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $sec⁡(-x+4\pi )=-10.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following statements regarding the graph of $y=\sec x$ are true?

- The function takes the value $1$ at $x = 2n\pi,$ where $n$ is an integer

- The range of the function is $(-\infty,+\infty)$

- The function has zeros at $x = 0, \pm \pi, \pm 2 \pi,\dots$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's have a look at the graph of $y=\sec x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934039/assets/da729794a0331383debd75be0a4ce4a9f2d4da3286f50bd4f284868996077412.png)

Let's go through each statement.

- The secant takes the value $1$ at $x =  2 n\pi .$ Therefore, statement I is true.

- The range of $f(x) = \sec x$ is $(-\infty,-1] \cup [1, \infty)$. Therefore, statement II is false.

- The secant graph does not intersect the $x$-axis. Therefore, statement III is false.

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Utilizing the Periodicity Property of the Secant Function
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The period of $y = \sec x$ is $2\pi.$ Therefore, for integer $n$ we have

$$
\sec{x} = \sec{(x+2n\pi)} .
$$

Substituting $n=4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}sec⁡x & =sec⁡(x+2\cdot 4\cdot \pi ) \\  & =sec⁡(x+8\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\sec{x} = 2\sqrt 2,$ then $\sec{(x+8\pi)} = 2\sqrt 2.$
